content.content:
**Missing or unrequested `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` response header**

Section 2.2, step 11.2 says that if the client sent protocols, the response must acknowledge one:

> "If protocols is not the empty list and extracting header list values given Sec-WebSocket-Protocol"
> "and response’s header list results in null, failure, or the empty byte sequence, then fail the WebSocket connection."

So if the client offered protocols and the response has no usable `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header, the client must fail the connection.

The page distinguishes this from the RFC 6455 check, which covers the unrequested case:

> "That only covers a subprotocol not requested by the client."
> "This covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server."

The page does not quote the RFC 6455 steps for an unrequested subprotocol, so this response can't describe them.

**Cookies and credentials**

Section 2 introduces the Fetch integration:

> "This way CSP, cookies, HSTS, and other Fetch-related protocols are handled in a single location."

Step 2 of section 2.2 sets the handshake request's credentials mode:

> The request's credentials mode is `include`.

The page contains Chromium networking source code (`net/socket/client_socket_pool_manager.cc`), base64-encoded. Decoded, the per-group limit is:

```cpp
std::array<size_t, kSocketPoolTypesSize> g_max_sockets_per_group =
    std::to_array<size_t>({
        6,   // kNormal
        255  // kWebSocket
    });
```

The accompanying comment says:

> "Default to allow up to 6 connections per host. Experiment and tuning may try other values (greater than 0)."

> "WebSocket connections are long-lived, and should be treated differently than normal other connections."

> "Use a limit of 255, so the limit for wss will be the same as the limit for ws."

So the limit is 6 for normal connections and 255 for WebSocket connections. The setter `set_max_sockets_per_group_for_test` enforces a ceiling of 512 and requires the value to be no greater than the soft cap per pool.

content.content:
**Failure:** On iOS 13, connections using a self-signed certificate failed. Normal HTTPS connections worked, but the **WebSocket connection failed**. The browser console showed "OSStatus -9807," which means errSSLXCertChainInvalid. Pierre Ossman reported it on 2019-10-16, moved from bug 7394.

**Certificate issues:** The reporter said the certificate was failing three iOS 13 requirements:
- Subject Alternate Name (SAN) not set properly
- Extended Key Usage (EKU) not set
- Validity period too long (3 years)

**Fix:**
- **SAN was the key change.** Ossman wrote: "After some testing it turns out that Subject Alternate Name is the critical missing piece." Adding it made the connection work.
- **EKU was a conflict.** Omitting EKU worked in some browsers but failed Apple's requirements. Removing Basic Constraints broke iOS trust, so it wasn't a fix either.
- **Workaround:** Upstream (Mozilla and Chromium) said the NSS EKU problem wasn't worth fixing. They suggested Netscape's legacy certificate type instead: "They did provide us with a better workaround though, in the form of Netscape's legacy certificate type."
- **Validity:** The content doesn't say whether the 3-year validity period was changed.

**Resolution and dates:**
- 2019-10-16: Reported; SAN identified as the fix the same day.
- 2019-10-18: Samuel Mannehed confirmed the dummy cert worked on iOS 13 Safari but failed in Chrome on Fedora 30.
- 2019-10-21: Root cause analysis of the NSS/EKU problem; issues reported upstream.
- 2019-10-22: Ossman reported the legacy certificate type workaround working in Chrome and Firefox (Linux), Safari (iOS and macOS), and IE and Edge (Windows).
- 2019-10-23: Alex Tanskanen retested and confirmed it works. The bug was closed as FIXED, targeting milestone 4.11.0.

**Title:** "We should log the reason when a secure wss WebSocket connection could not be established"

**Status/Resolution:** NEW, with no resolution set. It is unassigned, at P2 priority and Normal severity, in WebKit's Web Inspector component.

**Latest comment dates:** The most recent comment is Comment 5 (2014-08-03), which only links a Radar report. The last substantive comment is Comment 4 (2010-07-05).

**Accepted certificate and wss:// in Safari:** Comment 3 (2010-07-05) by Martyn Loughran reports that it works in Safari after accepting the certificate:

> "after changing the setting to always trust this certificate the WebSocket connection worked"

The reporter was using Safari 5 and a WebKit nightly. The comments don't mention iOS at all, and they don't explicitly say macOS, though the pywebsocket setup paths suggest a Mac.

**Logging request:** Comment 4 by Alexey Proskuryakov says:

> "Logging is absolutely what we should do."

He also cautioned against a bypassable warning sheet, saying that "providing an easy way to bypass security equals to having no security at all."

**Requirements for all TLS server certificates (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15):**

- Key size: "TLS server certificates and issuing CAs using RSA keys must use key sizes greater than or equal to 2048 bits." RSA certificates with smaller keys are no longer trusted for TLS.
- Hash algorithm: "TLS server certificates and issuing CAs must use a hash algorithm from the SHA-2 family in the signature algorithm." SHA-1-signed certificates are no longer trusted for TLS.
- Server name: "TLS server certificates must present the DNS name of the server in the Subject Alternative Name extension." Names in the CommonName are no longer trusted.

**Additional requirements for certificates issued after July 1, 2019:**

- "all TLS server certificates issued after July 1, 2019" must meet the following:
- Extended key usage: "TLS server certificates must contain an ExtendedKeyUsage (EKU) extension containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID."
- Validity period: "TLS server certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer" (measured from NotBefore to NotAfter).

**Scope:** The page applies these requirements to TLS server certificates and issuing CAs. It does not say anything about self-signed certificates, user-added roots, or system roots.

**Consequence:** "Connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail." The page says this may cause network failures, app failures, and websites not loading in Safari.

**Title:** "[websocket] does not send client certificate" (WebKit bug 158345)

**Status and dates:**
- **Status:** NEW. No resolution is listed, so the bug is still open.
- **Reported:** 2016-06-03 by Adi Stadelmann
- **Last modified:** 2021-07-23
- **Priority/Severity:** P2 / Normal

**What it says about wss connections and client certificates:**
- The reporter found that the SSL handshake fails because the client certificate is never sent, and that Firefox, Chrome, and Edge handled the same setup. The report was tested against a WebKit nightly build on OS X.
- Tor Arne Vestbø's analysis (2018) found that WebSocket connections are set up in the Network process, which has code for proxy credentials but "nothing for client certificates." He also noted that a normal page load must come first: "You need to do a normal page load first, and then do websocket requests after accepting the cert in the UI."
- He also reported that Chrome and Safari would not accept a self-signed server certificate without a Subject Alternative Name (SAN), and he shared an OpenSSL command that adds one.
- Alex Christensen (2018) said the best fix would be to reimplement WebSockets on NSURLSessionStreamTask, but he warned that this is a large change with high regression risk.
- Youenn Fablet (2020) said work was ongoing to use the NSURLSession WebSocket API. Tobias later reported that it can be enabled through Develop > Experimental Features in Safari 13.1 and iOS 13.4.1.
- Andreas Jung (2020) reported that on iOS 13.5 the client-cert WebSocket connection worked only once per browser start and failed after a refresh.
- Dirkjan Bussink (2020) reported that the NSURLSession WebSocket feature broke WebSockets on Big Sur and iOS 14 betas because of a faulty per-message deflate implementation.
- Brian Peiris (2021) said the bug blocks apps that need both WebSockets and protected APIs like getUserMedia, which require a secure origin, so self-signed certificates are the only option for them.

**Key quotes:**
- Alex Christensen (2018): "I think the best way to solve this would be to re-implement WebSockets using NSURLSessionStreamTask instead of CFReadStreamRef/CFWriteStreamRef."
- Youenn Fablet (2020): "There is ongoing work to use NSURLSession WebSocket API instead of the internal WebSocket implementation."
- Alexey Proskuryakov (2020): "Please feel encouraged to file bugs about any new issues that you may encounter with the experimental implementation."
- Brian Peiris (2021): "This issue is a blocker for developing webapps that need to use both WebSockets and protected APIs like getUserMedia."

The algorithm in § 3.1 (step 3) reads:

> "If origin's scheme is either "https" or "wss", return "Potentially Trustworthy"."

Nothing in that step checks the host, so an `https` origin with an IP-address host is potentially trustworthy regardless of which address it is. The only IP-specific rule is step 4, which covers loopback ranges (`127.0.0.0/8` and `::1/128`) for any scheme.

The document doesn't mention certificate validity or user override of certificate errors. Section 7.2 lets users configure origins as trustworthy, but it applies to development environments and isn't described as a certificate-error override.

| Version | Byte Mode, L | Byte Mode, M |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 106 | 84 |
| 6 | 134 | 106 |
| 7 | 154 | 122 |
| 8 | 192 | 152 |
| 9 | 230 | 180 |
| 10 | 271 | 213 |
| 11 | 321 | 251 |
| 12 | 367 | 287 |

The page does not include module width or size for any version, so I can't provide those values.

**Missing or unrequested `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` response header**

Section 2.2, step 11.2 says that if the client sent protocols, the response must acknowledge one:

> "If protocols is not the empty list and extracting header list values given Sec-WebSocket-Protocol"
> "and response’s header list results in null, failure, or the empty byte sequence, then fail the WebSocket connection."

So if the client offered protocols and the response has no usable `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header, the client must fail the connection.

The page distinguishes this from the RFC 6455 check, which covers the unrequested case:

> "That only covers a subprotocol not requested by the client."
> "This covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server."

The page does not quote the RFC 6455 steps for an unrequested subprotocol, so this response can't describe them.

**Cookies and credentials**

Section 2 introduces the Fetch integration:

> "This way CSP, cookies, HSTS, and other Fetch-related protocols are handled in a single location."

Step 2 of section 2.2 sets the handshake request's credentials mode:

> The request's credentials mode is `include`.

**Bug 235873**, "CSP: Improve compatibility of source matching," is **RESOLVED FIXED**. EWS closed it on 2022-04-02 after commit r292266 landed on main. It was reported on 2022-01-30 and last modified on 2022-04-02.

The WebSocket issue is tracked in duplicate bug 201591, titled "CSP "connect-src" 'self' does not match web socket scheme as per spec." Brent Fulgham marked it a duplicate of this bug on 2022-03-15. The patch changes scheme matching so that the 'self' source covers WebSocket schemes under the spec's rules. Patrick Griffis said the tests "covers http->wss and http->ws which is the majority of this change." The default-port changes were removed from the patch.

The page doesn't name a Safari version. It records the fix only as a WebKit Nightly commit (r292266), so I can't tell you which Safari release includes it.

The page contains Chromium networking source code (`net/socket/client_socket_pool_manager.cc`), base64-encoded. Decoded, the per-group limit is:

```cpp
std::array<size_t, kSocketPoolTypesSize> g_max_sockets_per_group =
    std::to_array<size_t>({
        6,   // kNormal
        255  // kWebSocket
    });
```

The accompanying comment says:

> "Default to allow up to 6 connections per host. Experiment and tuning may try other values (greater than 0)."

> "WebSocket connections are long-lived, and should be treated differently than normal other connections."

> "Use a limit of 255, so the limit for wss will be the same as the limit for ws."

So the limit is 6 for normal connections and 255 for WebSocket connections. The setter `set_max_sockets_per_group_for_test` enforces a ceiling of 512 and requires the value to be no greater than the soft cap per pool.

**Failure:** On iOS 13, connections using a self-signed certificate failed. Normal HTTPS connections worked, but the **WebSocket connection failed**. The browser console showed "OSStatus -9807," which means errSSLXCertChainInvalid. Pierre Ossman reported it on 2019-10-16, moved from bug 7394.

**Certificate issues:** The reporter said the certificate was failing three iOS 13 requirements:
- Subject Alternate Name (SAN) not set properly
- Extended Key Usage (EKU) not set
- Validity period too long (3 years)

**Fix:**
- **SAN was the key change.** Ossman wrote: "After some testing it turns out that Subject Alternate Name is the critical missing piece." Adding it made the connection work.
- **EKU was a conflict.** Omitting EKU worked in some browsers but failed Apple's requirements. Removing Basic Constraints broke iOS trust, so it wasn't a fix either.
- **Workaround:** Upstream (Mozilla and Chromium) said the NSS EKU problem wasn't worth fixing. They suggested Netscape's legacy certificate type instead: "They did provide us with a better workaround though, in the form of Netscape's legacy certificate type."
- **Validity:** The content doesn't say whether the 3-year validity period was changed.

**Resolution and dates:**
- 2019-10-16: Reported; SAN identified as the fix the same day.
- 2019-10-18: Samuel Mannehed confirmed the dummy cert worked on iOS 13 Safari but failed in Chrome on Fedora 30.
- 2019-10-21: Root cause analysis of the NSS/EKU problem; issues reported upstream.
- 2019-10-22: Ossman reported the legacy certificate type workaround working in Chrome and Firefox (Linux), Safari (iOS and macOS), and IE and Edge (Windows).
- 2019-10-23: Alex Tanskanen retested and confirmed it works. The bug was closed as FIXED, targeting milestone 4.11.0.

**Server doesn't support ALPN or omits the extension (Section 3.1):** The server isn't required to respond to the extension. Servers that receive it "MAY return a suitable protocol selection response to the client," and the ServerHello extension is likewise optional. The RFC doesn't say what the client should do when no ALPN response arrives, so it doesn't explicitly confirm that the client proceeds without a negotiated protocol. That outcome seems to follow from the optional design, but it's my inference, not stated text.

**When `no_application_protocol` is sent (Section 3.2):** The alert is sent only when the server supports none of the protocols the client advertised. In that case, the server must respond with a fatal alert. Otherwise, the server should choose its most preferred protocol that the client also offered.

The search didn't turn up anything specific to iOS 17 or 18, but several reports describe the exact symptom you're seeing: HTTPS works, WSS fails, and manually trusting the certificate doesn't fix it.

- **Matching symptom:** One developer found that the iOS browser accepted the cert for HTTPS, but not WSS. Another reported that an attempt to establish a wss:// connection towards a server that uses a self-signed certificate will result in an empty error.
- **Trust settings don't help:** A GitHub gist says manually installing the certificate doesn't help. A Cockpit project page says Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS and iPadOS does not support the WebSocket Secure sessions which Cockpit needs to function when using a self-signed or otherwise invalid certificate, even when they are manually marked as trusted.
- **Error messages:** Reports include OSStatus Error -9807: Invalid certificate chain and a message saying the certificate for the server is invalid.
- **Workarounds:**
  - Use a certificate issued by a trusted CA. The Cockpit page says installing a valid certificate should resolve this issue.
  - Use a self-signed root CA, trust it fully, and sign the server certificate with it. One gist reports this makes WebSocket connections work, though it's still completely homebaked.
  - Enable Apple's newer WebSocket framework in Safari's experimental settings. The Cockpit page says it does work as expected.
  - Switch to Socket.IO, which can fall back to HTTPS polling. One developer did this successfully.
- **Newer reports:** A developer reported WSS failing on iOS 26 beta 3 even though the certificate was accepted and the page loaded over HTTPS, so this may not be fixed in newer versions.

The sources are mostly community posts and forum threads from several years ago, so they don't confirm how iOS 17 and 18 behave specifically. Apple's own documentation on this would be the authoritative check, and I didn't find it in this search.

The search didn't turn up anything specific to iOS 17 or 18, but several reports describe the exact symptom you're seeing: HTTPS works, WSS fails, and manually trusting the certificate doesn't fix it.

- **Matching symptom:** One developer found that the iOS browser accepted the cert for HTTPS, but not WSS. Another reported that an attempt to establish a wss:// connection towards a server that uses a self-signed certificate will result in an empty error.
- **Trust settings don't help:** A GitHub gist says manually installing the certificate doesn't help. A Cockpit project page says Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS and iPadOS does not support the WebSocket Secure sessions which Cockpit needs to function when using a self-signed or otherwise invalid certificate, even when they are manually marked as trusted.
- **Error messages:** Reports include OSStatus Error -9807: Invalid certificate chain and a message saying the certificate for the server is invalid.
- **Workarounds:**
  - Use a certificate issued by a trusted CA. The Cockpit page says installing a valid certificate should resolve this issue.
  - Use a self-signed root CA, trust it fully, and sign the server certificate with it. One gist reports this makes WebSocket connections work, though it's still completely homebaked.
  - Enable Apple's newer WebSocket framework in Safari's experimental settings. The Cockpit page says it does work as expected.
  - Switch to Socket.IO, which can fall back to HTTPS polling. One developer did this successfully.
- **Newer reports:** A developer reported WSS failing on iOS 26 beta 3 even though the certificate was accepted and the page loaded over HTTPS, so this may not be fixed in newer versions.

The sources are mostly community posts and forum threads from several years ago, so they don't confirm how iOS 17 and 18 behave specifically. Apple's own documentation on this would be the authoritative check, and I didn't find it in this search.

content.content:
**Symptom:** On iOS 11 (not iOS 10), Mobile Safari sometimes fails to load some of the `<script src>` files from an HTTPS server that uses a self-signed certificate. The failures are intermittent and the set of failing files changes on each attempt. The problem appears most often when Safari is force-quit and reopened, which restores the same page. The author's test page should print 19 "X" lines and end with "19," but affected loads show fewer. Waiting and refreshing usually produces the correct result until Safari restarts. Developer tools sometimes show: *"Failed to load resource: The certificate for this server is invalid."*

**Cause:** The thread does not confirm a cause. The author's speculation is:

> "When Safari starts, it will try to load the list of accepted untrusted ssl certificates in a background task. For some reason, accessing this list and loading this list is not correctly synchronized so that during a short period after starting Safari, a check will be made against the list although is has not been fully loaded and the loading of some referenced resources will then fail because the untrusted certificate used is not found in the incompletely loaded list."

The "parallel connections each needing the certificate override" idea is not in the thread. It is a plausible hypothesis that fits the symptoms, but it is not what the author proposed.

**Fix:** None is given. The author reported the bug through Apple's Bug Reporter (Problem ID 36238559) and got no response. The only workaround the author found is to avoid self-signed certificates:

> "You need to actually create your own local CA (Certificate Authority), install this CA's public certificate on the iPad, manually enable that it is trusted as a CA, then use this CA to create an SSL certificate and then install and use this SSL certificate in IIS."

The thread has one reply, from another user (Anil Katakam, May 2018), which only asks: "You got any solution for this?" No answer appears in the thread.

**Fix:** The original poster (apankrat) got it working with a self-signed certificate, not a CA-signed one. The page doesn't mention a SAN.

- **What didn't work:** Trusting the server cert on iOS and changing the certificate's CN to the machine's IP address. The poster reported that the CN change "also made no difference."

- **Dec 29, 2020:** jech wrote "Not an issue with Galène" and closed the issue.

content.content:
**1. What makes a connection "secure"?** The draft leaves this to the user agent. Section 4.1.2.5 says the Secure attribute limits cookies to "secure" channels, where "secure" is defined by the user agent, and the typical case is HTTP over TLS. Section 5.7 uses the same wording for the check that rejects Secure cookies on non-secure requests. The examples use `https://` origins, but the draft gives no explicit scheme rule.

**2. Cookies for IP address hosts.** The draft doesn't address this directly. Section 5.1.3 says the suffix rule of domain matching applies only when "the string is a host name (i.e., not an IP address)." So a Domain attribute containing an IP address would match only that exact host. Without a Domain attribute, Section 5.7 sets the host-only-flag and uses the canonicalized request host as the cookie's domain. Nothing in the text excludes IP hosts from this, but that is an inference, not something the draft states.

**3. SameSite=Strict and same-site requests.** Section 4.1.2.7 says a Strict cookie "will only be sent along with 'same-site' requests." Section 5.2 defines a same-site request as one that is not a UI-triggered reload and whose current URL's origin is same-site with the client's "site for cookies." The draft does not mention WebSocket handshakes, so it does not say how they are classified. Applying the Section 5.2 criteria to a handshake would be an inference.

The search turned up related history, but no current Chromium bug report that matches your exact symptom, so treat this as background rather than a confirmed diagnosis.

- **Chrome's older behavior:** A 2011 WebKit mailing-list thread says that, in Chrome, a user's acceptance of a server's certificate also covered wss:// connections, while Safari and WebKit still failed the wss:// connection after the user accepted the https:// warning. As issue 41419 states, this will fail in Safari and WebKit (r87480.) Chrome on the other hand, consider the user's acceptance of the server's identity as valid for both wss:// and https:// connection.
- **The Chromium fix for the gap:** A Chromium code review (BUG=364361) describes the problem as the new WebSocket implementation being unable to handle sites with self-signed certificates and other cases where the user had overridden certificate errors. The patch added code to pass the SSL error up to the content layer so the override could be honored, and it landed in revision 275066. I did not confirm the exact release or whether it fully resolves your case.
- **Related reports:** A Qt forum post describes the same symptom, a wss:// connection failing with a self-signed certificate error even though the https:// page loads, and links an old Chromium issue (146848) that was marked WONTFIX. Mozilla's bug 1187666 for Firefox was also closed as WONTFIX.

The search found Safari and WebKit reports that match your symptom most closely. I found no Chrome-specific SameSite=Strict WebSocket bug from recent years.

- **Safari (WebKit bug 232666):** Strict cookies were left out of WebSocket requests in tabs restored or loaded from cache, such as after history navigation or reopening a closed tab. The report says this was seen on Safari 14 and 15 and appears fixed in 15.1, though the reporter could not find the fixing change. The bug page now shows a "resolved, configuration changed" status, so I could not confirm the current state. SameSite Strict cookies are not sent via WebSocket on any restored/cache-loaded tabs.
- **Safari developer forum thread:** A developer saw Safari skip Strict cookies on a reconnect to a secure WebSocket server, while the same setup worked in Chrome and Firefox. Removing HttpOnly made Safari work, so the bug seems tied to that combination. The developer confirmed the setup works fine on Chrome/Firefox.
- **WebKit bug 200345:** A reproduction showed Strict cookies sent on XHR requests but not on WebSocket requests in the same tab. A fresh top-level navigation restored them. This matches the bug 232666 behavior.
- **Firefox (Android, bug 1573860):** This is a different cause. Address-bar navigation used a null origin, so Strict cookies were withheld until the user navigated by clicking a link. The blog post says Both F3A and Firefox for desktop supports SameSite=Strict just fine. This is an HTTP cookie issue, not specifically a WebSocket one.
- **Chrome:** The only Chrome report I found is an old Wave Protocol issue from Chrome 7 beta (around 2010) where cookies were not sent to WebSocket servers. It is not SameSite-specific and is probably outdated.

Practical takeaway: if the failure happens only after a restored or cached Safari tab, or only after an address-bar navigation in Firefox for Android, these reports fit. Testing with a fresh top-level navigation is a quick way to check. I did not find a current status for these bugs, so check the WebKit and Mozilla trackers directly for the latest version.

content.content:
**Title:** "Can't connect to WSS/SSL websocket server with a self-signed certificate"

**Status:** RESOLVED, WONTFIX. The bug was opened about 11 years ago and closed about 10 years ago. It was filed against Core :: Security: PSM.

**Mozilla staff position:** Patrick McManus, who wrote much of the relevant code, said a failed wss:// load is a failed subresource, and Firefox doesn't show dialogs for those. He wrote that "https:// and wss:// require certificate validation - the hostname is never enough." He pointed to a stored exception as the way to pass validation: "You can either have a certificate that is validated via the PKI or you can use a stored exception for validation."

**Does a tab exception for the same host:port make wss:// work?** Yes, according to the thread. McManus suggested adding the exception by visiting the HTTPS address first: "You can add the exception by going to https://localhost:8080/ first." The reporter then confirmed that after adding the exception at 8080, the connection succeeded. The reporter said the expected behavior was a prompt when the page on port 9000 tried to connect, which Firefox did not show. A later user (not Mozilla staff) said the same workaround works for a non-localhost address (1.2.3.4:9000).

# Facts for issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port

Worktree `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/da9387bb` at `7fe8949`. No spike: every runnable question is settled by a source or the tree, and the rest need the owner's phone.

## Settled

Tree: `src/adapters/remote.rs:102-110` (`CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`); rcgen 0.14.10 defaults `not_before` 1975, `not_after` 4096 (`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:83-85`). Apple: https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769. The vendor tracker that agrees: ThinLinc bug 7401 (iOS 13 Safari: HTTPS page loaded, the WebSocket failed with `-9807` until a SAN was added; closed FIXED 2019-10-23) https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=7401. WebKit bug 158345 (2018 comment: Chrome and Safari refuse a self-signed server certificate without a SAN) https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345.
Queries: "Apple TLS server certificate requirements subject alternative name 398 days self-signed Safari proceed anyway"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate wss WebSocket fails after accepting certificate warning".

**Chrome applies the owner's certificate click-through to `wss://` on the same host; Firefox applies a stored exception for `https://host:port` to `wss://` on that host and port, and shows no dialog for a WebSocket by itself.**

Queries: "Chrome WebSocket wss self-signed certificate proceed override applies to WebSocket after clicking through interstitial chromium bug"; "Firefox wss WebSocket self-signed certificate exception added for https host works bugzilla".

**A browser that sent `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` fails the connection when the 101 does not echo one of the offered values.**
WHATWG WebSockets §2.2 step 11.2: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ ("if protocols is not the empty list and extracting header list values ... results in null, failure, or the empty byte sequence, then fail the WebSocket connection"); Chromium's handshake helper enforces the same (search result, cobalt mirror of `web_socket_handshake_helper.cc`). `respond_upgrade` echoes nothing today: `src/adapters/remote.rs:519-526`.
Query: "WebSocket Sent non-empty 'Sec-WebSocket-Protocol' header but no response was received RFC 6455 server must echo subprotocol".

**The browser WebSocket handshake carries cookies (credentials mode `include`); a `Secure` cookie is sent on what the user agent deems secure, typically TLS, with no rule about the host being an IP; a cookie without `Domain` is host-only on the request host, IP or not; `SameSite=Strict` is sent on same-site requests.**
WHATWG WebSockets §2.2 step 2; RFC 6265bis §4.1.2.5, §4.1.2.7, §5.1.3, §5.7: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis. An `https` origin is "potentially trustworthy" by scheme alone, host unchecked: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1 step 3. `history.replaceState` needs no secure context, only a same-origin URL: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState.
Safari caveat, vendor tracker: Strict cookies were missing from WebSocket handshakes in tabs restored without a top-level navigation (Safari 14 and 15, reported fixed in 15.1): https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232666, https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200345. A cookie set on the fetch reply to `/pair`, not on a 101, avoids the Safari `HttpOnly`-on-101 report (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488).
Queries: "Secure cookie IP address origin self-signed certificate browser secure context WebSocket sends cookie"; "SameSite=Strict cookie not sent WebSocket handshake Chrome Firefox Safari bug".

**CSP `connect-src 'self'` matches a same-host `wss://` in Chrome (since 2018), Firefox, and WebKit since r292266 (2022-04-02, bug 235873, duplicate 201591); older Safari needs the scheme or origin listed.**
https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=235873; https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=201591; MDN's note: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src.
Query: "Content-Security-Policy connect-src 'self' websocket wss same origin CSP3 Safari Firefox".

Tree: `src/adapters/remote.rs:567`, `699-706`. Safari's figure (6) comes only from a vendor-neutral table (DiffusionData docs), a lead.
Query: "browser maximum connections per host HTTP/1.1 Safari Chrome Firefox 6 connections".

**rustls with no `alpn_protocols` ignores the client's ALPN offer and sends no alert, so a browser offering `h2` completes the handshake and speaks HTTP/1.1; RFC 7301 §3.1 makes the server's ALPN response optional and §3.2 reserves `no_application_protocol` for a server that supports ALPN with no overlap.**

Query: "rustls server no alpn_protocols configured client offers h2 ALPN handshake succeeds HTTP/1.1 fallback RFC 7301".

**The URL form of the invite is 153 bytes, the JSON form 189; `qrcode` 0.14 picks the smallest version at level M, so the URL is version 9 (53 modules, 180 byte capacity) and the JSON version 10: the QR gets smaller, not larger.**
`QrCode::new` → `EcLevel::M` and `encode_auto` (`qrcode-0.14.1/src/lib.rs:75-94`); capacity table https://www.thonky.com/qr-code-tutorial/character-capacities; lengths computed from `CODE_LENGTH` 8 (`src/adapters/remote.rs:321`), a 64-hex key, a 36-char UUID, `192.168.100.100:50000`. Query: "QR code capacity version 7 8 byte mode error correction M 160 characters".

**`read_request` can keep more headers: it already parses every header into `headers` and drops them when the struct is built; the only test of it asserts method, path, `lines`, bearer and body (`a_request_reads_with_its_query_bearer_and_body`), so adding fields breaks nothing.** `src/adapters/remote.rs:444-514`, tests at `1045-1062`.

**`hide_workers` applies to `projects`, `sessions` and `waiting` replies without `scope=all`; a page reading those needs nothing more.** `src/app.rs:2687-2698`, called at `3119-3121`.

**With `listen.lan` off the port binds `127.0.0.1`; `/info` does not carry `listen`, so a page cannot tell, and need not: a phone cannot reach a loopback bind at all.** `src/app.rs:2962-2966`, `remote_info` `3568-3604`.

## Unresolved

**Whether Safari on iOS and iPadOS applies the owner's certificate click-through to `wss://` once the certificate has a SAN.** Tried: WebKit bug 41419 (2010, macOS Safari 5: works after "always trust"); Cockpit's documentation (undated, https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari) says Safari's default WebSocket on iOS, iPadOS and ARM Macs fails with a self-signed certificate "even when manually marked as trusted" and recommends a valid certificate or the experimental NSURLSession WebSocket; ThinLinc bug 7401 says a SAN made it work on iOS 13; Galène issue 18 and a gist (2020) say only a leaf signed by a device-trusted CA worked; an Apple forum thread (iOS 26 beta 3, `wss://192.168.1.81`, "resolved in beta 5") https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842. The sources disagree and none names the certificate's SAN. Queries: the two under the first Settled claim and "Safari iOS 17 OR iOS 18 self-signed certificate WebSocket wss fails Show Details visit website accepted HTTPS works WebSocket does not" (extended). Line the plan builds to: the page must work without the socket, polling `revision` through REST on a timer when `/api/v1/events` fails to open, and the certificate gets a SAN, `serverAuth` EKU and a validity of 825 days or fewer regardless; if the owner's phone opens the socket, the poll is only the fallback.

**Whether a SAN for an IP address survives the Mac changing address.** An `iPAddress` SAN names one address; `local_address()` returns one outward route (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-971`). No source consulted. Line: the plan either reissues the certificate from the same key when the listen address changes (safe for native pins, above) or puts a DNS name in the SAN and serves the URL under that name; either way the identity's key does not rotate.

**Whether Safari's per-host connection limit is 6.** Only a vendor-neutral table. Line: size the unauthenticated pool for 6 per browser plus the native clients, or count strangers per source address; the pool of 4 is too small for one browser either way.

## For the owner

**Does the iPhone's Camera open `https://<ip>:<port>/?code=...` in Safari from the QR?** Apple's guide says "tap the link to open the content" without naming link types (https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT208843). If yes, scanning is the whole flow; if no, the owner types the URL from the dialog's text, which the plan must show in full either way.

**After the certificate warning on the phone, does `/api/v1/events` open under the SAN'd certificate?** If yes, live updates; if no, the REST poll above carries the page, and the dialog says so.

**Does the one address in the URL route to the phone on the owner's network?** If yes, one URL; if no, the dialog must list every non-loopback interface's address, which the plan can do from `if_addrs` or a `getifaddrs` wrapper, and the QR keeps the first.

**Is a version 9 QR at 4 px per module readable from the Mac's display by the phone?** If yes, `QR_SCALE` stays; if no, raise it (`src/ui/remote.rs:41`); the dialog width 620 holds up to 8 px.
